theme: O LORD, God of vengeance, the cry for justice
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 94. It is a prayer to the God of vengeance for the oppressed. Notice how it moves from complaint to teaching, and from anxiety to the comfort of God’s steadfast love.
settingTheScene: Psalm 94 has no title. It is a communal and personal lament, and it is also a wisdom psalm, with a section that instructs the arrogant. The enemies are oppressors within the covenant community, who “kill the widow and the sojourner, and murder the fatherless.” It is the third of the psalms of justice in this unit.
observation: “O LORD, God of vengeance, O God of vengeance, shine forth!” (v. 1).
“Rise up, O judge of the earth; repay to the proud what they deserve!” (v. 2).
“How long shall the wicked, O LORD, how long shall the wicked exult?” (v. 3).
“They kill the widow and the sojourner, and murder the fatherless; and they say, The LORD does not see” (vv. 6-7).
“He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eye, does he not see?” (v. 9).
“Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O LORD, and whom you teach out of your law” (v. 12).
“When I thought, My foot slips, your steadfast love, O LORD, held me up” (v. 18).
“When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul” (v. 19).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a bold double address: “O God of vengeance.” The word “vengeance” here means just retribution, the action of a judge who puts things right. It is not petty revenge. The psalmist asks God to “shine forth,” to appear as a judge and deal with the proud.

The complaint is fully honest. The wicked exult. They boast. They crush God’s people. And they say, “The LORD does not see.” This is the arrogance of those who think no one is watching. The psalmist answers them with a rhetorical question: “He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eye, does he not see?” It is the answer of logic. The Creator of ears and eyes must himself hear and see. God’s knowledge is not less than ours but infinitely greater.

Then the psalm shifts to a more personal note. “Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O LORD, and whom you teach out of your law, to give him rest from days of trouble.” A person who is taught by God finds rest even in times of trouble. This is a different way to see suffering: as a place of instruction. The psalmist knows that the LORD will not forsake his people.

The center of the psalm’s comfort is verses 18 and 19. “When I thought, My foot slips, your steadfast love held me up.” The psalmist’s footing was failing. And God’s covenant love caught him. And when the cares of his heart multiplied, God’s consolations cheered his soul. The word “cares” can mean also “anxious thoughts.” When anxieties pile up, God’s comfort is greater.

The psalm ends in confidence: “The LORD has become my stronghold, and my God the rock of my refuge. He will bring back on them their iniquity.” God will deal with the wicked in his own time. Meanwhile, he is a refuge.
connection: Jesus said that nothing is hidden that will not be made known (Luke 12:2-3), and that the Father sees in secret (Matthew 6:4). Hebrews 12:5-11 draws on this teaching about discipline. Philippians 4:6-7 speaks of casting anxieties on God. 1 Peter 5:7 says, “Casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.” 2 Corinthians 1:3-5 describes God as the Father of mercies and God of all comfort.
application:
When anxious thoughts multiply, pray verse 19 and let God’s consolations cheer you.

Ask whether you ever act as if God does not see. Bring any hidden thing to him.

Thank God that when your foot slips, his steadfast love holds you up.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to shine forth against injustice.
Thank him that when your foot slips he holds you.
Ask him to console you when cares are many.
